# VTOP vs Apache Kafka: measured

<!-- Generated by benchmarks/kafka_compare/report.py from the committed CSV. Do not edit by hand: change the generator or re-run the benchmark. -->

> **Single host, Apple M5 Max (), Docker Engine - Community; indicative, not a production benchmark.** Both clusters ran as Linux containers in the same Docker Desktop VM, one at a time, with identical per-node limits. Treat the numbers as a relative reading on a laptop, not as capacity figures for either system.

Phase 1 of [#595](https://github.com/allamiro/vtop-engine/issues/595) ([#596](https://github.com/allamiro/vtop-engine/issues/596) throughput and latency, [#600](https://github.com/allamiro/vtop-engine/issues/600) charts). Raw data: [`results.csv`](../run/results.csv) and [`environment.json`](../run/environment.json), run `schema4-runner`. Every measured number on this page and in the images (tables, charts, ratios) is generated from that CSV, and the stated conditions (machine, limits, images, commit, matrix, dates) from that `environment.json`, by `benchmarks/kafka_compare/report.py`.

## Method

- **Same machine, same limits (rule 1).** Three Kafka brokers (KRaft, combined broker+controller) and three VTOP nodes, each a container with 2 CPUs and 2g of memory, no swap, data on named volumes on the Docker VM's disk (`/dev/nvme1n1 ext4`). One system runs at a time; each cell starts from empty volumes.
- **Same client (rule 2).** `kafka-producer-perf-test/kafka-consumer-perf-test 4.3.2 (JVM)` from `apache/kafka:4.3.2@sha256:852a0d49fc4e656b022e7f23785411802c9a088c78a7c5e39f33969de9c227a7`, in its own container (4 CPUs, 4g), pointed at each cluster in turn. Producer properties set: `acks=all compression.type=none`; everything else is the client's default for both (its own config dump for each system is in `environment.json` under `observed.producer_config`).
- **Same replication contract (rule 3).** Kafka: RF=3, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`. VTOP: one range replicated to three nodes, acknowledged at a write quorum of 2 of 3 (`Durability::Quorum`), `acks=all` from the client.
- **Profile `defaults` (rule 4).** Each system as shipped. This is **not** durability parity: Kafka acknowledges once the in-sync replicas have the batch in their page cache (`flush.messages` unset), while a VTOP quorum acknowledgement means two replicas have **fsynced** the append. The `fsync-parity` profile (Kafka with an fsync after every message, `flush.messages=1`) is measured for Kafka in the end-to-end runs only, at the same offered rate as the others; see *What each durability profile costs in latency*.
- **VTOP's group commit (#752).** VTOP ran with `group_commit: {enabled: false}` and `group_commit: {enabled: true}` in the leader's node config, written explicitly for each setting (a change of the node's default cannot change what a setting means), and the node's own `vtop_broker_group_commit_enabled` gauge was read to confirm it before anything was timed. Every other VTOP setting is the same in each. Kafka has no counterpart, so it ran once and is one series; each VTOP row names its setting in the CSV's `group_commit` column.
- **Open-loop latency (rule 6).** Latency comes from fixed offered rates (`--throughput`) at 25%, 50%, 75% of **Kafka's** median saturation for the cell, offered to both systems. A run more than 5% short of its offered rate is flagged *not sustained*: the tool's throttle then becomes a closed loop and its latency understates the real one, so the chart draws such points hollow and joins no line through them.
- **Repetition (rule 7).** 1 repetitions per measurement; the first 20% of each run's records are warm-up (`--warmup-records`) and excluded, after an unrecorded warm-up run per cell. Tables show the median with the min-max across repetitions.
- **Correctness first.** Before any timing, each fresh cluster took 10 records of the cell's size with `acks=all` and handed every one back, byte-exact and in order, through the same client; a cluster that failed would have been refused.

## Group commit ablation

VTOP's produce throughput at saturation with the node's `group_commit.enabled` off and on (#752): the same cells, the same client, one VTOP cluster brought up fresh per setting. `on / off` is the ratio of the two medians (the ranges are in the throughput table above). It says how far the setting moved the cell, not why; a ratio near 1 means it did not. This run had 1 producer. The last three columns are the leader's own counters for the `on` runs.

| record size | group commit off records/s | group commit on records/s | on / off | mean group size (on) | overlapped (on) | ms per request (on) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 B | 6,000 (6,000-6,000) | 6,000 (6,000-6,000) | 1.00x | - | - | - |

How to read it:

- **One producer cannot show group commit.** A group can only hold requests that are in the broker at the same
  time, and one producer never has two there: the gateway's session loop answers a Produce request before it
  reads the next one from that connection, and the gateway's bridge to the broker queues an idempotent
  producer's record sets one after another (the producer turnstile). So with one producer every group is one
  request, and the setting can only show its own cost; a ratio near 1 there is the expected result, not
  evidence that group commit does nothing. Several producers on one partition (`--producers N`: separate
  connections, separate producer ids, one range) are what can share a barrier.
- **Partitions do not merge.** A group is formed per range: each partition is its own range with its own
  leader log and its own coordinator, and fsyncs of different logs cannot be shared. Several partitions are
  not evidence for or against group commit.
- **Pipelining one producer's requests is not built.** Letting one connection have several record sets in
  flight before the earlier one is durable (answered in order) is the only change that could move the
  1-producer cell; it is not part of group commit and does not exist yet.
- **Several producers in one row.** A row's records/s and MiB/s are what all its producers delivered over one
  shared window, from their common start to the last one's end, not the sum of their own rates, which would
  overstate a row whose producers finish at different times.
- **The counters.** `mean group size` is the leader's `vtop_broker_group_commit_requests_total` over
  `vtop_broker_group_commits_total`; `overlapped` is the share of groups whose local append and fsync ran
  while the previous group replicated (`vtop_broker_group_commit_overlapped_total`); the last column is
  `vtop_broker_produce_phase_seconds_total` per phase (local fsync / replicate / commit) over the requests, so
  a time shared by a group is divided among its requests. Each is read on the leader before and after every
  saturation repetition of the `on` setting, summed over the repetitions; the window includes the tool's
  warm-up records, which it produces and leaves out of its own rate. With group commit off the node exports
  no request count, so the off runs' phase totals stay in `environment.json` under
  `observed.vtop_produce_counters`. A dash is a cell whose counters were not read (named in `events`).

## Reading the results

Where Kafka is faster, the reasons known from the code and the configuration are these. Except for group commit (2), which the ablation above measures, none of them was
isolated by a separate measurement in this phase; they are the explanation the code supports, not a proof.

1. **What an acknowledgement costs.** Under `defaults`, a Kafka `acks=all` acknowledgement waits for the
   in-sync replicas to have the batch in their logs (page cache); nothing is fsynced. A VTOP quorum
   acknowledgement waits until a majority of the three replicas, the leader counted, has made the append
   *durable* (fsync), and the leader has advanced the committed high-water mark. Every produce request pays
   for fsyncs and a replication round trip before it is answered. This is the largest single difference, and
   it is a difference in the guarantee as much as in speed; the `fsync-parity` end-to-end runs (*What each durability profile costs in latency*) price the
   same guarantee on Kafka.
2. **Group commit on the gateway path.** The node's group commit (`group_commit.enabled`, #752: one fsync
   and replication round shared by concurrent produce requests on a range) is a setting, and this run measured
   VTOP with it off and on, so its effect on these cells is in the tables above, not argued from the code. The
   client caps a request at `batch.size` (16 KiB by default) whatever the record size, and one connection has
   one request in the broker at a time, so a ceiling set per request shows up as a roughly constant MiB/s
   across record sizes and a record rate that falls as records grow; whether sharing a barrier lifts that
   ceiling depends on how many requests are in the broker at once, which is what the ablation reads out.
3. **Translation in the gateway.** Every Kafka record batch is decoded, validated (CRC, attributes) and
   re-appended through the native broker, which frames it again for the replica plane; Kafka validates the
   batch and appends it with offsets assigned in place, without taking its records apart. The cost is CPU and
   copies, not round trips.
4. **Fetch path.** Kafka serves a fetch from stored batches with a zero-copy file transfer; the gateway reads
   records through the native broker and re-encodes them as a Kafka record batch.

This run records each system's CPU seconds and bytes written (*CPU and bytes written*, above), so whether the produce path is bound by CPU or by durability round trips can be read from the run's own counters rather than from a probe.

**On the latency chart:** where VTOP's saturation is below the lowest offered rate (25% of Kafka's), no VTOP
fixed-rate run can be sustained, and the perf tool's throttle degenerates into a closed loop against a full
producer buffer. Those VTOP latencies are queueing in the client (seconds), not VTOP's service latency at that
load; they are drawn hollow and must not be read as "VTOP's p99 at 25% load". A fair open-loop VTOP latency
curve needs offered rates below VTOP's own saturation, which the issue's Kafka-relative rule does not produce
here; the end-to-end runs are offered a rate relative to the slower system's saturation for that reason.

Nothing here measures what VTOP adds over Kafka on this path (fenced epochs, the verified commit rule, the
evidence chain; see [COMPARISON.md](../COMPARISON.md)), and nothing here is a failover, archive or crash
measurement (#597, #598, #599).

## Gateway gaps met (rule 10)

| gap | met by | exact error | what was done |
|---|---|---|---|
| CreateTopics | kafka-topics.sh --create | `UnsupportedVersionException: The node does not support CREATE_TOPICS` | The VTOP topic is the range in the node config; Kafka's is created by run.py with kafka-topics.sh. |
| DescribeConfigs | kafka-topics.sh --describe | `UnsupportedVersionException: The node does not support DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` | Not needed by the perf tools; the topic layout is recorded from the node config instead. |
| OffsetCommit (no metadata plane) | kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh with auto-commit on | `Offset commit failed on partition bench-0 at offset <n>: The message format version on the broker does not support the request (gateway: "kafka OffsetCommit refused: this gateway has no durable offset store")` | enable.auto.commit=false for BOTH systems; reads are measured, commits are not. |
| Compressed batches | producer with compression.type=zstd | `UnsupportedCompressionTypeException: batch 0: record batch is compressed (codec 4), which this gateway does not decompress` | compression.type=none for both systems; compression is out of phase 1. |
| Gateway on followers | vtop-node with a `kafka` block on a follower | `the node refuses a kafka block on any role but leader or standalone (the gateway is served by a leader or standalone only)` | The gateway runs on the range's leader only; one partition means one gateway. |

## Known gaps in this phase

- **Matrix size.** Record sizes 100 B only; 1 partition, 1 producer, no compression, profile
  `defaults` in every mode, and `fsync-parity` for Kafka's end-to-end runs only. #596's full matrix (10 KiB, 6 partitions, 4 producers, zstd) is not run.
- **One gateway, one partition.** The gateway runs on the range's leader only; a multi-partition VTOP topic
  needs one leader per partition and is not exercised here.
- **No metadata plane.** VTOP runs as a static leader with two followers (live-chaos scenario 17's shape), so
  there is no lease, no failover and no durable consumer-offset store; Kafka runs its full KRaft quorum. Neither
  matters to a steady-state produce/fetch measurement, but the two clusters are not doing identical background
  work.
- **Latency resolution.** The JVM perf tool reports percentiles in whole milliseconds, from a sample of the
  run's records; sub-millisecond differences are invisible.
- **End-to-end latency and cpu and bytes written** (#596 metrics 3 and 4) are measured at one offered load per cell, not as a curve. End-to-end latency has the resolution of a record's `CreateTime`, 1 ms.
